The Use of Dietary Supplements 
Many people take supplementary vitamins and minerals – usually tablets taken 
daily in additionto a regular diet. The scientific evidence to support this practice 
is now being questioned 
 
 
A 
For decades scientists have searched for evidence that vitamin C will protect us from 
colds and flu, and have mostly come up empty-handed – there’s more evidence that 
regular hand-washing will stop us catching a cold. So why, according to one recent 
survey in a western country, do more than 30% of people still take vitamin C or other 
supplements? Here’s one useful guideline: beware the phrase ‘scientific studies show’ 
when used about a product that is for sale. Scientific studies are complicated, mean 
little in isolation, and generally only make sense to people used to reading them – and 
even they can’t always agree. 
 
B 
‘One of the things that people seem to hate about science is that one week we’re saying 
one thing, and the next week another expert says something that completely 
contradicts that,’ says Mark Bolland, a senior researcher at the University of 
Auckland. The truth is that not all scientific studies are created equal. The most 
revealing type of study would be a randomised trial, when researchers take a group of 
people, divide them in half and give one group a supplement and the other a placebo. 
Drug companies are legally obliged to conduct such trials for new medicines. But 
companies selling supplements have no such obligations, and generally point to 
observational studies. However, observational trials just follow a group of people who 
are taking supplements anyway – usually educated females inclined to look after their 
health. Their better health, then, may have less to do with supplements and more to do 
with the people taking them, thus accounting for some of the apparent contradictions. 
 
C 
Here is something scientists do know: excessive quantities of life-giving consumables – 
water, oxygen, vitamins – can be dangerous. Recently, the Journal of the American 
Medical Association published the results of a randomised trial looking at whether 
supplements could protect against serious disease. The trial, involving 35,000 men, 
was eventually stopped after it seemed that taking the supplement had no benefits, 
and might even increase the risk of disease. One of the largest studies was conducted 
by the Cochrane Collaboration, which looked at 67 randomised trials on supplements. 
It found none of the supplements improved health, but vitamins A, E and beta-
carotene were associated with an increased risk. ‘As far as I’m aware,’ says Rod 
Jackson, professor of epidemiology at the University of Auckland, ‘none of the recent 
randomised controlled trials has shown any benefits of vitamins. Folic acid before and 
during pregnancy appears to be one of the few exceptions.’

7 
 
D 
The research into calcium supplements reflects much of the wider debate. An 
influential study published in the 1990s showed that calcium supplements reduced the 
risk of hip fractures by 40%. However, the sample for the study was women of a single 
nationality whose bones and lifestyle were unrepresentative of the wider population, 
which was the cause of some criticism. Studies that followed weren’t quite as 
persuasive, though they did show that calcium supplements improved bone density, 
which researchers believed might reduce the number of fractures. This, however, was 
an assumption, so Ian Reid, professor of medicine and endocrinology at the University 
of Auckland, decided to find out if it was actually true. Using a large, randomised 
study, Reid’s results were confounding: calcium made little difference to bones, was 
beneficial to cholesterol and blood-pressure levels, but also seemed to be associated 
with an increased risk of heart failure. 
 
E 
To ensure these results were reliable, one of Reid’s team members, researcher Mark 
Bolland, began gathering all the data from existing trials and confirmed Reid’s 
discovery. Neither of these studies was well received in some other quarters, including 
by some scientists. But, says Bolland, ‘…two years later, no-one has yet disproved it.’ 
What people want to know, though, is whether women should take calcium 
supplements. Bolland replies that it depends on your definitions: to his mind, safety is 
about weighing things up carefully. In the case of calcium supplements, there are 
possible serious side effects, so they cannot be recommended. Evidently, local general 
practitioners have taken the results on board; in the last six years, says Bolland, 
prescriptions of calcium have dropped by 60 per cent. 
 
F 
Calcium isn’t the whole story, though. Currently the most fashionable supplement isn’t 
a vitamin or mineral, but a long-chain fatty acid, known as omega-3. We can’t 
manufacture it synthetically but we can get it from our diet, mainly from oily fish like 
tuna or from fish-oil capsules. Victoria University professor Shaun Holt recommends 
omega-3, in fish or supplementary form. ‘There’s evidence that omega-3s are good for 
over 30 health conditions, and the evidence that they are good for your heart is rock 
solid,’ says Holt. Welma Stonehouse, associate professor of human nutrition at Massey 
University, agrees. She’s sceptical about most dietary supplements, but takes omega-3 
regularly. Murray Skeaff, professor of human nutrition at the University of Otago, is 
also not convinced about the value of taking supplements. He says, ‘There is a massive 
accumulation of evidence to show if you want to prevent disease and prolong life, the 
best way to do it is having a good diet. The evidence for supplements just pales in 
comparison.’

Questions 14 – 18 
Reading Passage 2 has six paragraphs, A-F. 
Which paragraph contains the following information? 
Write the correct letter, A-F, in boxes 14-18 on your answer sheet. 
NB        You may use any letter more than once. 
14 
a mention of a study that was abandoned to protect the health of participants 
 
15 
a warning that the use of certain language can be misleading 
 
16

17 
a reference to a scientist checking the research findings of a colleague 
 
18 
a reference to a scientist who personally uses a supplement

Questions 19 – 22

Write the correct letter, A-E, in boxes 19-22 on your answer sheet. 
NB        You may use any letter more than once. 
19 
One group of people may benefit from taking a specific supplement for a limited period 
of time. 
 
20 
Scientists have failed to show that controversial research findings were incorrect. 
 
21 
Science shows that the food people eat every day is the most important factor for 
being healthy. 
 
22 
The general public are tired of scientific studies appearing inconsistent.

Research into Calcium Supplements 
A study published in the 1990s showed calcium may strengthen hip bones, though there was 
criticism that the sample of women was 23 ............ . Professor Ian Reid investigated whether 
calcium supplements increased the 24 ............ of bones, and thus reduced the number of 
fractures. His results showed that calcium had little effect on bones, improved some aspects 
of health but also caused problems with the 25 ............ – results that were unpopular with 
some scientists. Mark Bolland says that, based on how he defines safety, he wouldn’t 
recommend taking calcium supplements. His view seems to be shared by local doctors, given 
that 26 ............ for the supplement have fallen sharply recently.
